idea: Prepare the target in $|-\rangle$. Then the single oracle call writes $f(x)$ as a sign $(-1)^{f(x)}$ on the input branch instead of as a bit on the target. This is called phase kickback. The input ends up as $|+\rangle$ when $f(0)=f(1)$, and as $|-\rangle$ up to a global sign when they differ. A final $H$ turns that sign pattern into a measured 0 or 1.
circuit:
input   |0> --H--[     ]--H-- measure: 0 = constant, 1 = balanced
                 [ U_f ]
target  |1> --H--[     ]----- stays |->, not measured

idea: The oracle marks the answer by negating its amplitude. Diffusion then replaces every amplitude $a_x$ with $2\bar a-a_x$, a reflection about the mean $\bar a$. That shrinks the unmarked amplitudes and grows the marked one. With four labels, one round reaches certainty. With $N$ labels and one answer, about $(\pi/4)\sqrt N$ rounds are needed, and extra rounds overshoot.
circuit:
bit 0  |0> --H--[     ]--[           ]-- measure
                [ O_f ]  [ diffusion ]      (one round for N = 4)
bit 1  |0> --H--[     ]--[           ]-- measure

idea: This is Deutsch's kickback trick applied to $n$ input bits at once. Because $f_s(x)=s\cdot x$ is a parity, the sign pattern $(-1)^{s\cdot x}$ factors into one state per bit: $|-\rangle$ where $s$ has a 1, and $|+\rangle$ where it has a 0. One Hadamard per bit converts each of those into the matching bit of $s$, so a single query reveals all $n$ bits.
circuit:
x0  |0> --H--[     ]--H-- measure -> s0
x1  |0> --H--[ U_f ]--H-- measure -> s1
x2  |0> --H--[     ]--H-- measure -> s2
y   |1> --H--[     ]----- stays |->, not measured

idea: The circuit is the same as Bernstein–Vazirani, but the question is different. After the query and the final Hadamards, every input $x$ contributes $(-1)^{f(x)}/N$ to the amplitude of the all-zeros output, where $N=2^n$. A constant function gives amplitude $\pm1$ there, so the result is always all zeros. A balanced function cancels it to exactly 0, so the result is never all zeros.
circuit:
x (n bits)  |0...0> --H--[     ]--H-- measure: all zeros = constant
                         [ U_f ]                   otherwise = balanced
y           |1>     --H--[     ]----- stays |->, not measured

idea: Simon uses equal-output pairs instead of signs. The output register starts at zero and records $f(x)$, which groups the inputs into pairs $\{x,x\oplus s\}$. The final Hadamards make each pair's two paths cancel on every $y$ with $s\cdot y=1$. So each run returns a random $y$ satisfying $s\cdot y=0$. About $n$ runs give $n-1$ independent equations, and classical elimination over bits solves them for $s$.
circuit:
x (n bits)  |0...0> --H--[     ]--H-- measure y   (y . s = 0)
                         [ U_f ]
f (n bits)  |0...0> -----[     ]----- ignored
repeat about n times, then solve the equations classically

idea: This is Grover's method with any reversible preparation circuit $A$ in place of the Hadamards. Negate the good candidates ($S_f$), then reflect about the prepared state $A|0\rangle$ ($R_s$). Each round rotates the state by $2\theta$ toward the good part, where $\sin\theta=\sqrt a$. In the worked example $a=1/4$, so $\theta=\pi/6$ and one round reaches success probability 1. For small $a$, about $1/\sqrt a$ rounds replace the roughly $1/a$ tries of measure-and-retry.
circuit:
|0> --[ A ]--( [ S_f ] then [ R_s ] ) repeated j times-- measure

R_s = A (2|0><0| - I) A^dagger : undo A, reflect about all-zeros (negate every other label), redo A
